problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.statement: Rotate an n × n matrix 90° clockwise in-place. You must do this without allocating another matrix.
problems.understanding: A 90° clockwise rotation maps matrix[r][c] → result[c][n-1-r]. Instead of allocating a new matrix, two sequential in-place operations achieve the same result: first transpose (flip across the main diagonal), then reverse each row.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Allocate a second matrix, copy cells to their rotated positions, then copy back.

problems.intuition:
Two in-place operations compose to give a 90° rotation:

① Transpose: swap matrix[r][c] with matrix[c][r] for all r < c.
② Reverse each row: call row.reverse().

No extra memory needed.
problems.approach:
1. Transpose: for r in range(n), for c in range(r+1, n): swap matrix[r][c] ↔ matrix[c][r].
  2. Reverse rows: for each row in matrix: row.reverse().
problems.takeaway: Pattern — 90° clockwise = Transpose + Reverse rows (counter-clockwise = Transpose + Reverse columns)

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.statement: Given an m × n matrix, return all elements in spiral order.
problems.understanding: Track four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. Process the outermost ring in four sweeps (→ ↓ ← ↑), then shrink boundaries inward and repeat.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Use a visited boolean matrix and change direction when hitting a boundary or visited cell.

code.py:
class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix):
        rows = len(matrix)
        cols = len(matrix[0])
        visited = [
            [False] * cols
            for _ in range(rows)
        ]
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        result = []
        r = c = direction = 0

        for _ in range(rows * cols):
            result.append(matrix[r][c])
            visited[r][c] = True

            nr = r + directions[direction][0]
            nc = c + directions[direction][1]

            if (
                nr < 0 or nr >= rows
                or nc < 0 or nc >= cols
                or visited[nr][nc]
            ):
                direction = (direction + 1) % 4
                nr = r + directions[direction][0]
                nc = c + directions[direction][1]

            r, c = nr, nc

        return result

problems.intuition: Maintain four boundary variables. Process the current ring's four edges in order, then shrink each boundary inward. Guard against single-row or single-column cases before the ← and ↑ sweeps.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize top=0, bottom=rows-1, left=0, right=cols-1.
  2. While top <= bottom and left <= right:
  3. → Append matrix[top][left..right]; increment top.
  4. ↓ Append matrix[top..bottom][right]; decrement right.
  5. ← If top <= bottom: append matrix[bottom][right..left] reversed; decrement bottom.
  6. ↑ If left <= right: append matrix[bottom..top][left] reversed; increment left.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Four shrinking boundaries — process outermost ring, collapse inward, repeat

problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problems.statement: Given an m × n matrix, if any cell is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in-place.
problems.understanding: Store which rows and columns need zeroing — but use the matrix itself as the storage. The first row and first column act as marker arrays. Handle them separately at the end.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Use two sets to record which rows and columns contain zeros, then zero them.

problems.intuition: Repurpose matrix[0][c] and matrix[r][0] as markers for columns and rows. Pre-check if the first row or column itself contains a zero so they can be handled last without ambiguity.
problems.approach:
1. Check first_row_zero = any(matrix[0][c] == 0 for c) and first_col_zero = any(matrix[r][0] == 0 for r).
  2. For r in 1..rows, c in 1..cols: if matrix[r][c] == 0, set matrix[r][0] = 0 and matrix[0][c] = 0.
  3. Zero rows 1..rows where matrix[r][0] == 0.
  4. Zero cols 1..cols where matrix[0][c] == 0.
  5. If first_row_zero: zero entire row 0. If first_col_zero: zero entire col 0.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Use the input matrix itself as metadata — repurpose first row and column as markers

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.statement: A number is happy if repeatedly replacing it with the sum of the squares of its digits eventually reaches 1. Return True if the number is happy.
problems.understanding: An unhappy number never reaches 1 — it enters a cycle. The process of digit-squaring is a value transformation that either terminates at 1 or loops. Floyd's cycle detection handles both cases without storing visited states.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Keep a seen set; stop when 1 is reached or a repeated value is detected.
complexity: Time: O(log n) — bounded digit states

problems.intuition: Model the transformation as a linked-list-style sequence. A happy number converges to the cycle 1 → 1 → …; an unhappy number enters another cycle. Floyd's slow/fast pointers detect the cycle in O(1) space.
problems.approach:
1. Define next_number(num): extract digits, return sum of their squares.
  2. Initialize slow = n, fast = next_number(n).
  3. While fast != 1 and slow != fast: advance slow one step, fast two steps.
  4. Return fast == 1.

optimal.title: Optimized Code (Python 3)
complexity: Time: O(log n) — bounded digit states

problems.takeaway: Pattern — Repeated value transformation → cycle or termination → Floyd's Cycle Detection (same family as LC 141)

problems.title: Plus One
problems.statement: Given a large integer represented as a digit array, increment it by one and return the result as a digit array.
problems.understanding: Incrementing from right-to-left naturally handles carry propagation. The only edge case: if all digits are 9, every digit becomes 0 and a new leading 1 must be prepended.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Reconstruct the integer, add 1, convert back to a digit array.

problems.intuition: Walk right-to-left. If the digit is < 9: increment it and return immediately (carry stops). If it is 9: set it to 0 and continue (carry propagates). If we exhaust the array, prepend a 1.
problems.approach:
1. Iterate i from len(digits)-1 down to 0.
  2. If digits[i] < 9: increment and return digits.
  3. Else: set digits[i] = 0, continue.
  4. After the loop (all 9s case): return [1] + digits.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Right-to-left carry propagation — stop as soon as carry disappears

problems.title: Pow(x, n)
problems.statement: Implement pow(x, n) — raise x to the power n. n may be negative.
problems.understanding: Multiplying x by itself n times is O(n). Binary exponentiation observes that x^n = (x²)^(n/2), halving the exponent each step — this gives O(log n).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Multiply x by itself n times in a loop.

problems.intuition: If n is even: x^n = (x²)^(n//2) — square x and halve n. If n is odd: multiply the current x into result first, then halve. Negative n → invert x.
problems.approach:
1. If n < 0: set x = 1/x, n = -n.
  2. Initialize result = 1.
  3. While n > 0: if n % 2 == 1, multiply result *= x.
  4. Square: x *= x; halve: n //= 2.
  5. Return result.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Binary Exponentiation — halve the exponent at each step by squaring the base

problems.title: Multiply Strings
problems.statement: Given two non-negative integers as strings, return their product as a string. You may not convert them to integers directly.
problems.understanding: Digit i of num1 multiplied by digit j of num2 contributes to position i+j+1 in the result array (of size n+m). Propagate carry leftward to position i+j.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Convert both strings to integers, multiply, return the result as a string. (Violates the problem constraint but useful baseline.)

problems.intuition: Simulate elementary-school long multiplication. Use a result array of size n+m. For each pair of digits at indices (i, j), add their product to result[i+j+1] and propagate the carry to result[i+j]. Strip leading zeros at the end.
problems.approach:
1. Return '0' if either input is '0'.
  2. Allocate result = [0] * (n + m).
  3. Nested loops i from n-1 to 0, j from m-1 to 0.
  4. product = int(num1[i]) * int(num2[j]); add to result[i+j+1].
  5. Carry: result[i+j] += result[i+j+1] // 10; result[i+j+1] %= 10.
  6. Strip leading zeros and join digits into a string.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — String arithmetic — position array: digit[i] × digit[j] maps to index i+j+1, carry propagates to i+j

problems.title: Detect Squares
problems.statement: Design a data structure that supports add(point) and count(point). For count, return the number of axis-aligned squares that can be formed using the query point as one corner.
problems.understanding: For a query point (x, y) and a diagonal point (x2, y2) to form an axis-aligned square: |x2-x| == |y2-y| (non-zero). The other two corners are then (x2, y) and (x, y2). Count = product of frequencies of all three non-query corners.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Store all points in a list; for each count query, scan all pairs and check the square condition.
complexity: add: O(1), count: O(P) — P = distinct points

problems.intuition: Group points by their x-coordinate. For each unique x2 ≠ x, the diagonal candidate's y value must be exactly y ± side where side = |x2 - x|. Only two candidate y2 values need checking — constant per x2.
problems.approach:
1. Store self.points = defaultdict(Counter) where self.points[x][y] = frequency.
  2. add(x, y): self.points[x][y] += 1.
  3. count(x, y): iterate over all distinct x2 in self.points (skip x2 == x).
  4. side = abs(x2 - x). Check y2 ∈ {y + side, y - side}.
  5. For each valid y2: answer += points[x2][y2] × points[x][y2] × points[x2][y].
  6. Return answer.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Coordinate frequency map — axis-aligned square: |Δx| == |Δy|; count = product of three corner frequencies
